content.text:
The file had no artwork to improve. It was a single empty root tag, so I rewrote it as a valid, scalable, accessible scaffold. I could not run a validator because the permission policy blocked it, so I confirmed well-formedness by inspection only.

Before:

```xml
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"/>
```

After:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     width="100"
     height="100"
     viewBox="0 0 100 100"
     role="img"
     aria-labelledby="svg0-title">
  <title id="svg0-title">Untitled graphic</title>
  <!-- Drawing content goes here. The coordinate system runs 0 to 100 on both axes. -->
</svg>
```

What each change fixes:

- **Coordinate system.** The original had no `viewBox`, so browsers would render a fixed default box and the graphic could not scale. It now has a square 0 to 100 space.
- **Intrinsic size.** Width and height give the file a defined size when used as an image or in a layout.
- **Accessibility.** The image role and title give screen readers a name. Replace the placeholder title with a real description, or mark the SVG decorative with `aria-hidden="true"` if it should be skipped.
- **Encoding.** The XML declaration makes the encoding explicit for a standalone file.
- **Room to draw.** The self-closing tag is now an open and close pair with a comment marking where shapes go.

Three checks were blocked and not performed: a hex dump to look for hidden bytes, a read of the extended attributes to learn where the file came from, and an `xmllint` validation of the result. The hidden-byte check was not needed in the end, since the byte count matched the visible text exactly.

One thing to flag: if this file was supposed to contain a drawing, that content was already missing before I touched it. Re-export it from the original source, or tell me what it should depict and I will draw it into this scaffold.
